title: Bunk's counter-melodies for each tune
summary: Blumberg explains how Bunk played with quiet daring and built a counter theme for each tune, such as for Honeysuckle Rose.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Well, now Bunk had his, had his own way of playing, uh, these tunes. He, uh, particularly with the Stuyvesant band, he'd, uh, uh, he'd play a couple ensembles in and then, uh, then George would, uh, come in for a solo usually with Jim, the two of them. And Bunk might even keep playing real quietly. I used to get real close to the, to the horn. He'd point the horn down at the floor. And sometimes he'd just be moving the valves and I knew he was playing something and if only I could hear it. And I don't know, it always seemed to me that the prettiest things he ever played were the things that, that you could hardly hear. Yeah, some of those second hearts. He'd play little phrases that were just unbelievable. He'd wonder, did I hear it or not, you know. And just little turns and, and things. It, uh, it seemed to me he would play things more daring, you know, real quietly than he would loud. He, he, he actually had a very classical approach, a very formalistic approach to playing. And, uh, uh, uh, each chorus was constructed in a very clear, clear-cut way. And, uh, he had a, uh, a counter theme for each, uh, tune that, that he played. He, uh, he had a second theme. And he would play that, uh, generally after all the choruses. In other words, if there's gonna be two or three ensembles out, let's say after the piano chorus, that was the, that was the, the, uh, the comma in the middle of the sentence for that band, it was a piano chorus. And then Funk would, would come in with his, his secondary theme, which was, uh, uh, usually a beautifully conceived thing where it would, it would have pauses in the same places that the original tune had notes and it would have notes in the places where the, you know, the original, it would be a real counter melody, a beautiful counter. And, uh, it would have little turns and, and, uh, he would play that and, uh,
Without anybody else taking the straight melody.

No, sometimes he'd play it as an ensemble lead or sometimes he'd play it as a solo. Uh, yeah, without anybody else playing the straight melody. It would, and, uh, and then he sometimes he used that to take the thing out. In other words, he'd play that for two or three choruses in a row. And sometimes he'd, uh, he'd go to a simpler riff to take the thing out from that. Yeah. And, uh, I, I, one of the few things that I can remember musically was, uh, that had never been recorded, was the, I don't think it had been recorded, was the counter melody he used on Honeysuckle Rose, which was a very, uh, sounds like something Lenny Tristano might have written in Conception. It was very, uh, complex, uh, uh, very fine thing. Uh.
